annotations.text: TODAY. The resting TV's photos as they ship (development after #58), at 2:40 PM. A photo stays a minute and its only move is a 6% zoom over that minute, so from the sofa it reads as still. The line about the photo runs over the left photo of a pair, a bug that is fixed whichever is chosen.

A: EVERY PHOTO MOVES ITS OWN WAY. A photo every 18 seconds, each with its own slow move: in toward one side, a pan across, out from close, a lift. They dissolve through a soft blur. A photo taken upright shows alone, over a blurred, enlarged copy of itself. The board plays three times faster than the TV would.

FOR: The biggest change in feel for the least new: it is the same screen, alive. AGAINST: Nothing about the photos themselves; a folder played well.

B: A DAY OF PHOTOS PLAYS AS A LITTLE STORY. A's motion, and the photos taken on the same day play together: a title card first ("A day at the beach", the date, how many), three from the day as a collage, then each in turn. A photo taken on this date in an earlier year comes first that day, with "One year ago today" in lamp color. Flip between the three.

FOR: It feels like the household's own album, not a folder. AGAINST: A day's title has to come from somewhere: the date always, a place only if the phone kept one (which today's photos deliberately don't), so "A day at the beach" would usually be the date alone unless somebody names the day.

C: ONE PHOTO AT A TIME, FRAMED LIKE A PRINT. A white mat and a matte in the photo's own color, the clock small beside it, the facts as one line along the foot. Nearly still: it drifts against burn-in and changes every few minutes.

FOR: The calmest; looks like art on the wall, not a screensaver. AGAINST: The opposite of what was asked for: it makes the screen quieter, not livelier.

A: A CARD TAKES A TURN BETWEEN THE PHOTOS. About one card for every five photos, held about a minute: a note from a phone, a countdown, the house today (sunset, frost, the moon, the porch light), a fact, a trivia question (OK for the answer), a joke, a quote, or a public-domain painting. The clock goes small in the corner. Flip through them.

FOR: Each gets the whole screen, so each reads from the sofa. AGAINST: A card nobody wanted interrupts the photos; so each kind is a switch per screen (last page).

The words, facts and paintings would be curated sets that come with hub updates, checked before they ship: no outside service is called, and nothing is written by a model.

B: A TODAY CARD IN THE CORNER. The photos never stop; one glass card in the top corner turns over between a note, a countdown and a fact. Flip it.

FOR: Photos and news at once; nothing interrupts. AGAINST: A small card is a lot to read from three meters, a trivia question or a painting doesn't fit, and the card sits over every photo.

C: THE FAMILY BOARD. A screen can show this instead of photos: the notes as paper on a board, what's coming up, and one photo at a time in a frame beside them. It suits a kitchen or hallway screen more than the TV.

FOR: Everything the family left in one glance, like a fridge door. AGAINST: A different screen to keep, and it takes the photos off the big picture. Could sit beside A as a choice per screen rather than instead of it.

A: THE MORNING CARD. The first time a screen wakes after sunrise, or when a morning routine runs, it opens on Good morning: the line for the day, the weather in words, and what is waiting. A line somebody left last night takes the line's place, signed (flip it). After a few minutes, or a press, it goes back to the photos.

FOR: A real moment, once a day, and the family's own words when there are some. AGAINST: A whole screen for one line. The lines are curated sets: encouragement in the morning, rest at night, never preachy, not repeated for months; a verse of the day is an optional set.

B: THE MORNING LINE OVER THE FIRST PHOTO. The same line, laid large over the first photo of the morning, which then carries on as usual.

FOR: Lighter: the morning starts with a photo and a word, not a card. AGAINST: The line competes with the photo, and there is no room for the weather in words or a note.

EVERY DIRECTION: NIGHT. Bedtime (built) gains the evening line under its button. When Bedtime is pressed, the screen shows only that line for a few seconds, then the TV turns off, so the last thing seen is a kind word, not a list of lights. Flip to see after the press.

SAID ALOUD, in either morning direction: the morning line on the room's speaker, quietly, off unless a household turns it on, and only once somebody is up (a morning routine ran, or a tap). The hub never starts talking on its own.
TODAY. Photos as it ships (#58): a switch per screen for photos, and nothing else can take a turn.

A: EACH SCREEN HAS ITS OWN LIST. Photos becomes Your screens; tapping a screen opens its list: what it shows (photos, or the family board), how the photos play (one after another, or day by day), photos, notes and countdowns, the house today, a fact or trivia, jokes, quotes, art; a line for the day and saying it aloud; a verse and horoscopes, off to start.

FOR: The kitchen can be the family board and the TV the photos. AGAINST: Two levels where today there is one.

B: ONE LIST FOR THE HOUSE. Which screens show photos, as today; what comes between them is one list for every screen.

FOR: One page, the same everywhere. AGAINST: Every screen shows the same things, so a kitchen board (cards C) has nowhere to be chosen.

EVERY DIRECTION: WRITING THEM. From Your screens on a phone: a note (until tonight, tomorrow, or until somebody takes it down), a countdown (a birthday comes round every year), and a line for the morning, for everyone or one person's phone, which greets the first screen to wake tomorrow, signed, then goes.

WHY THIS EXISTS

20 November 2026, after #58: the photos on the TV look still from the sofa, and a resting screen could carry more than photos: fun cards, the family's own notes and countdowns, and a word in the morning and at night. Four questions, a page each: how the photos move, what takes a turn between them, the morning and night, and choosing it all on the phone.

Under all of them, as before: nothing holds still (burn-in), every word passes the readability check, the default suits kids, and every kind of card is a switch.

DECIDED 20 NOVEMBER 2026

PHOTOS: A and B, and each screen chooses (How the photos play: One after another, or Day by day). Both move every photo its own way.
CARDS: A, a card takes a turn between the photos; and the family board (C) is a choice per screen (What it shows: Photos, or The family board).
MORNING: A, the morning card, with the evening line on Bedtime and as the last thing on the screen.
PHONE: A, each screen has its own list, now with What it shows and How the photos play at the top.

The line about a photo running over a pair is fixed with the photos.

NOT CHOSEN

C made the screen calmer, which is the opposite of what was asked. The corner card (cards B) was small from the sofa; the line over a photo (morning B) left no room for the weather or a note; one list for the house (phone B) had nowhere to choose the family board.
